answer:
Don't pick one cause. Instead, ask the data which causes apply where, and fund in a way that doesn't depend on the answer.

## Why "pick the most likely cause" is the wrong frame

- **Chronic absenteeism is probably several problems under one label.** A student missing school because of a 70-minute bus ride, one avoiding a bully, and one whose family stopped prioritizing attendance after COVID all count as the same statistic. Each needs a different fix. Funding one cause will help one group and leave the others untouched.
- **The causes likely reinforce each other.** A student who misses school falls behind, which makes school more anxiety-provoking, which leads to more absences. Parents who see their kid struggling may stop pushing attendance. A bus problem can start the cycle and the others sustain it. Each stakeholder may be seeing a real piece of it.
- **Every stakeholder's claim is testable, and you probably already have the data.** The disagreement exists because no one has checked yet.

## Step 1: A 4–6 week diagnostic, run by someone neutral

Use a district analyst or outside partner, not the principals or the transportation office, who each have a stake.

| Claim | What to check |
|---|---|
| **Routes** | Compare absenteeism and tardies for students on cut or changed routes against similar students who weren't affected, before and after the change. "On-time performance" isn't the same as access. Look at walk distances, ride times, and stops eliminated. |
| **Bullying/climate** | Compare school-level absence rates with climate survey results, incident reports, and nurse or counselor visits. Check whether parent reports match logged incidents, since a gap suggests under-reporting. |
| **Anxiety/behind** | Look at whether grade or test declines come before the absences or after them. Check absence patterns (Mondays, specific class periods), health-office visits, and counseling referrals. |
| **Parent attitudes** | Survey parents, and compare how families respond to outreach. If personalized contact quickly brings kids back, attitudes matter. If it doesn't, something else is going on. |

Also look at these:
- **Variation across schools.** If some middle schools doubled and others didn't, compare them. That's your best natural experiment.
- **The timing of the rise.** Did the increase follow the route cuts, or the pandemic, which hit every district? Elementary and high school trends, and neighboring districts, are useful comparisons. If absenteeism doubled everywhere, routes alone can't explain it.
- **Student-level patterns.** How many chronically absent students were also absent in prior years? How many are new? What share are excused versus unexcused?
- **Reasons for absences.** Ask students and families directly through short interviews or surveys. Attendance codes are often unreliable.

Ask each stakeholder group now: "What evidence would change your mind?" That makes it harder to dismiss the findings later.

## Step 2: Fund no-regret actions while you diagnose

Some interventions work regardless of cause, so you can start them now:
- **An early-warning system** that flags students at 5–10% absence, well before the 10% chronic threshold.
- **Personalized family outreach.** Targeted letters and calls showing a family their child's absences have reduced absenteeism in several studies.
- **Mentoring or check-in programs** such as Check & Connect, aimed at the most at-risk students.
- **A school attendance team** in each building that reviews cases and matches students to supports.
- **Cleaner attendance data**, so you can learn from whatever you do.

## Step 3: Allocate the rest by evidence, with a learning design

When the diagnostic comes back, split money by how many students fall into each pattern: transportation fixes, anti-bullying and climate work, mental health and academic recovery supports, and family engagement. Roll out in some schools first or in phases, with comparison groups, so you learn what works rather than just spending.

## What to tell the board

Something like:

> "The evidence points to several causes, and we can't responsibly bet everything on one. We'll fund proven interventions now that help regardless of cause, complete a six-week diagnostic that tells us how to target the remaining funds, and measure results by school so we can adjust."

That is still a decision, with a date and a budget. It also protects you if the "most likely cause" turns out to be only 30% of the problem.

If your leadership truly insists on one cause, give them a ranked estimate from the diagnostic, with the share of absent students each cause plausibly explains. Don't rank by which stakeholder sounded most confident.

If it would help, I can draft the diagnostic plan, a board memo, or a data request list for your analysts.
